Humans, Art, Tools, and AI

A framework for applied creativity in the age of automated making

Chris Busse
busse@eszetthq.com · linkedin.com/in/chrisbusse

What is art?

Art and technology started as the same word.

  • Art Latin ars: skill, craft. From a root meaning “to fit together,” also in arm, article and harmony.[1]
  • Technology Greek technē: art, craft. From a root meaning “to weave,” also in text and textile.[2]
  • Artificial Latin artifex, an “art-maker”: made with skill, not found in nature.[3]

“Artificial intelligence” was named in 1955. It starts with ars.[4]

Ars Technē Artifex
  1. Harper, D. (n.d.). art (n.); *ar- “to fit together.” Online Etymology Dictionary.
  2. Harper, D. (n.d.). technology (n.); technical (adj.); *teks- “to weave, fabricate.” Online Etymology Dictionary.
  3. Harper, D. (n.d.). artificial (adj.); artifice (n.). Online Etymology Dictionary.
  4. McCarthy, Minsky, Rochester & Shannon (Aug. 31, 1955). A Proposal for the Dartmouth Summer Research Project on Artificial Intelligence.

Part I

Art & communication

67,800 years of making pictures and sending words.

≥ 67,800 years ago · Sulawesi

The oldest picture we can date is a hand.

Someone on Muna Island blew pigment around their hand, onto a cave wall.[1]

Muna lies just off southeast Sulawesi, in Indonesia. At Leang Karampuang, on Sulawesi, people painted a scene by 51,200 years ago: humans and a wild pig.[2]

Chauvet, c. 36,000 years ago.[3] Lascaux, c. 21,000 (often quoted as 17,000).[4]

  1. Oktaviana, A. A. et al. (2026). Rock art from at least 67,800 years ago in Sulawesi. Nature.
  2. Oktaviana, A. A. et al. (2024). Narrative cave art in Indonesia by 51,200 years ago. Nature 631, 814–818.
  3. Quiles, A. et al. (2016). A high-precision chronological model for the decorated cave of Chauvet-Pont d’Arc. PNAS 113(17).
  4. Ministère de la Culture (n.d.). Dating the figures at Lascaux.

c. 3300–3200 BCE · Uruk

Writing began as bookkeeping in clay.

Cuneiform: wedges pressed into wet clay with a cut reed.[1]

First it counted grain, beer and sheep. Within centuries it kept laws, letters, prayers and the first stories with an author’s name on them.

  1. Encyclopædia Britannica (n.d.). Cuneiform.

105 CE · Han China

Paper made marks cheap to carry.

Cai Lun reported a method to the Han court: bark, hemp and rags, pulped, lifted on a screen and dried.[1]

Older scraps of paper survive; his recipe is the one that spread, along the Silk Road to Baghdad and on to Europe.

  1. Encyclopædia Britannica (n.d.). Cai Lun.

c. 1450 · Mainz

The press made copying a machine’s job.

Gutenberg combined metal type, oil-based ink and a screw press. His Bible appeared c. 1455.[1]

Bi Sheng had set movable type in fired clay in the 1040s.[2]

Scribes copied one book at a time. Within fifty years, Europe’s presses had printed millions.

  1. Library of Congress (n.d.). The Gutenberg Bible. Bibles exhibition.
  2. Encyclopædia Britannica (n.d.). Movable type.

1827 · Saint-Loup-de-Varennes

Photography let light draw the picture.

Niépce’s view from an upstairs window took hours to expose.[1]

Daguerre’s process went public in 1839, and picture-making was no longer only for people who could draw.

  1. Harry Ransom Center (n.d.). The Niépce Heliograph. University of Texas at Austin.

May 24, 1844 · Washington to Baltimore

The telegraph cut the message loose from the messenger.

Morse tapped “What hath God wrought” down about 40 miles of wire.[1]

For the first time, words travelled faster than a horse, a ship or a train could carry them.

  1. Library of Congress (n.d.). Today in History: May 24. “What hath God wrought?”

March 1876 · Boston

The telephone carried the voice itself.

Bell’s patent was granted on March 7. Three days later he called to his assistant: “Mr. Watson, come here.”[1]

No operator, no code: just a person, talking.

  1. Bell, A. G. (1876). Improvement in Telegraphy. US Patent 174,465, granted Mar. 7, 1876.

December 28, 1895 · Paris

Film made pictures move, and gathered an audience.

The Lumières’ cinématographe was camera, printer and projector in one hand-cranked box.[1]

Their first paid screening, in a café basement, showed ten short films of everyday life.

  1. Encyclopædia Britannica (n.d.). Lumière brothers.

November 2, 1920 · Pittsburgh

Radio sent one voice to everyone at once.

KDKA broadcast the Harding–Cox election returns, the start of scheduled commercial radio.[1]

Reginald Fessenden later claimed a voice-and-music broadcast in 1906.

  1. IEEE (n.d.). Milestone: KDKA, First Commercial Radio Station, 1920. ETHW.

September 7, 1927 · San Francisco

Television’s first electronic picture was a straight line.

Philo Farnsworth’s image dissector sent a single line across his lab.[1]

John Logie Baird had demonstrated mechanical television in London the year before.[2]

  1. Encyclopædia Britannica (n.d.). Philo Farnsworth.
  2. Encyclopædia Britannica (n.d.). John Logie Baird.

1951–1963 · MIT and Boeing

Then a computer drew.

Whirlwind put pictures on a screen around 1951.[1] At Boeing in 1960, William Fetter and Verne Hudson named it “computer graphics.”[2]

In 1963, Ivan Sutherland’s Sketchpad let a person draw on the screen with a light pen.[3]

  1. Computer History Museum (n.d.). This Day in History: April 20 (Whirlwind).
  2. HistoryLink (n.d.). William Fetter, E.A.T., and 1960s Computer Graphics Collaborations in Seattle.
  3. Sutherland, I. E. (1963/2003). Sketchpad: A man-machine graphical communication system. UCAM-CL-TR-574.

Part II

The tools

What each of those stops put in a maker’s hands.

The tools · by hand

Pigment, clay, reed and brush.

For tens of thousands of years, the tool was in your hand, and so was the skill.

Cave Clay Paper

The tools · by mechanism

Type, lens and key.

Machines took over copying, seeing and sending. A person still chose what to print, frame and say.

Cave Clay Paper Press Camera Telegraph

The tools · by signal

Microphone, reel and tube.

Electricity carried voices and pictures to millions at once, and made new jobs: operator, projectionist, announcer.

Cave Clay Paper Press Camera Telegraph Telephone Film Radio

The tools · on a screen

Picture tube and light pen.

Then the picture became something a computer could draw, and a person could draw on.

Cave Clay Paper Press Camera Telegraph Telephone Film Radio Television Sketchpad

The tools

Every one of these was the new tool once.

Each arrived with a worry about what it would replace. Each still needed a person with something to make.

Cave Clay Paper Press Camera Telegraph Telephone Film Radio Television Sketchpad Next?

The machines were always coming for the jobs.

1930“We are being afflicted with a new disease… namely, technological unemployment.”[2]John Maynard Keynes, who added: “only a temporary phase”
1961“Automation may prevent the economy from creating enough new jobs.”[3]TIME, “The Automation Jobless”
1964“Jobs are disappearing under the impact of highly efficient, progressively less costly machines.”[4]Memo to President Johnson
1983“The role of humans as the most important factor of production is bound to diminish in the same way that the role of horses… was.”[5]Wassily Leontief, Nobel economist
1966“The basic fact is that technology eliminates jobs, not work.”[3]Johnson’s National Commission on Technology, Automation, and Economic Progress

What actually happened

Some people lost their jobs. The work grew.

PressScribes copied one book at a time.Book prices fell by two-thirds by 1500.[1] About 12.6M printed books by 1500, against about 5M manuscripts in the whole century.[2]
Talkies9,885 theater musicians, about half of them, displaced in two years, 1929–31.[3]The worriers were right about them. Sound film became an industry of its own.
Dial phonesOperators: about 342,000 mid-century[4], 3,430 today.[5] Those in the job moved to lower-paid work.The next generation’s employment didn’t fall: clerical and service jobs took them in.[6]
ATMsTellers per urban branch fell from 20 to 13, 1988–2004.Branches grew 43%, and teller jobs didn’t fall.[7] Mobile banking is doing what ATMs didn’t: −13% projected by 2035.[8]
Desktop publishingTypesetting became prepress: 23,840 jobs today.[5]The typesetter’s job moved to every desk: 253,100 graphic designers.[9]

Part III

The machines behind a picture

How much computer does it take to change a picture?

MS Paint · Photoshop · DALL·E

Three ways to change a picture.

The same job, editing an image, on one processor core, on a gaming card, or in a data center.

Paint shipped with Windows 1.0 in 1985.[1] Photoshop CS6, in 2012, was the last version you could buy outright.[2] DALL·E runs on servers of eight AI accelerators.[3]

Paint1985 PhotoshopCS6 · 2012 DALL·E2022–

The software

All three are programs. Who wrote the rules differs.

MS PaintPhotoshop CS6DALL·E
Written inC++ for WindowsC++, plus graphics-card codePython and PyTorch, plus graphics-card code
Rules written byProgrammers, line by lineProgrammers, line by line: millions of linesProgrammers wrote the learning code; the rules were learned from data
What’s insideFixed recipes: fill, line, resizeFixed recipes: blur, levels, Content-Aware FillModest code, and a model file of billions of learned numbers
Outside dataNone: only your imageYour image, and presets made by Adobe staffHundreds of millions of captioned images, used in training[1]

CS6’s Content-Aware Fill borrows patches from your own photo only. DALL·E’s exact code is unpublished.

  1. Ramesh, A. et al. (2022). Hierarchical Text-Conditional Image Generation with CLIP Latents. arXiv:2204.06125.

Same math, different authors

Both are just weighted sums.

Photoshop’s blur: nine numbers, chosen by a person

Each new pixel is its neighbors times these weights, divided by 16. An engineer picked them.

DALL·E: billions of numbers, set by training

The same multiply-and-add, over billions of weights. Training nudged each one until pictures matched their captions.

Dot area follows each number’s size: blue positive, ochre negative. The learned values here are illustrative.

A note on the numbers

Read these as orders of magnitude.

Estimates, not benchmarks

OpenAI doesn’t publish how many GPUs serve one image. We assume one to eight data-center GPUs.

Different kinds of math

CPU, graphics and AI “tensor” TFLOPS aren’t the same unit. The real-world gap is still thousands-fold.

The lines are blurring

Today’s Photoshop and Paint have AI features that send work to the cloud or an AI chip: DALL·E’s world.

A tool can’t mean anything

Art is morally human. AI is morally a tool.

A painting carries someone’s intent, choices and risk. A brush has none of those, and neither does a model.

“A computer can never be held accountable. Therefore a computer must never make a management decision.”[1]

We don’t credit the brush for a painting, or blame it for a bad one.

  1. Attributed to a 1979 IBM internal training page; original lost (via S. Willison, Feb. 3, 2025).

Human in the cockpit

The people who build it and use it own what it does.

  • Builders choose what it learns from, and what it refuses to make.
  • Makers choose what to make, what to keep, and what to put their name on.
  • Nobody gets to say “the AI did it.”

“Loop thinking creates blame cultures. Cockpit thinking creates ownership cultures.”[1]

Signed: a person
  1. Mishra, T. (n.d.). Time to retire “human-in-the-loop” and embrace “human-in-the-cockpit.” SingleStone.

Eszett

An idea, and then a room full of people.

January 2025 · The original concept

A talent agency for human artists

“Eszett is building a global talent agency for human visual artists who reject Generative AI in their work.”[1]

  • We run the artist’s shop: production, fulfillment, service, accounting, on an automation and AI back end.
  • Artists pay nothing; Eszett takes the risk and shares the revenue.
  • A bet on demand for “guaranteed human-made imagery.”

March 19, 2025 · rvatech/ Data + AI Summit

Launched at the rvatech/ Data + AI Summit, with artist Joshua Barber

We exhibited to about 500 people.[2] The conversations at that table started us toward product/market fit, and a slight pivot from the original idea.
